name: Felix Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Felix, thanks for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no connection to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Course. I'm a first-year apprentice carpenter with a regional builder, and we're putting up a retirement village on the old golf course off Station Road, forty bungalows and a main building. I'm mostly on roofs at the moment, lifting trusses into place, fixing bracing, battening out for the tilers. My dad drops me at the gate at seven on his way to the bus depot, he's a mechanic there. I like being up on a roof first thing when the mist's still on the fairways, it's peaceful.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said first-year apprentice. How did you come to it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Late. I left school at sixteen and did eight years in a frozen food warehouse, driving a forklift, nights mostly. I knew I'd regret it if I never learned a proper trade, so I started this at twenty-six on apprentice pay, which is a big drop. I've moved back in with my parents to make it work, I pay them board, and I've got maybe three weeks of money saved. I use AI now and then, mostly to check the maths for roof pitches when I'm revising for college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair enough. I won't lie, part of me would be glad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad I learned a trade, because it was never going to be a computer putting a roof on. I'd say it to the lads and to my mates from the warehouse. I'm not really online, maybe the odd comment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd make me feel like I made the right call. I took a pay cut to do this, everyone said I was mad at my age. If nothing changes, I've got time to finish, get qualified and start earning properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the apprenticeship and get my level two done. I'd keep living at home another two years and save a bit more, try for a hundred a month. Once I'm qualified, I'd look at going self-employed, doing roofs and extensions, maybe with my cousin Jun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did people say when you left the warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum cried, and not happy crying, because of the money. My mates thought I was having a midlife crisis at twenty-six. But my grandad was a carpenter back home, and he always said a man with a trade never goes hungry. That stuck with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just finishing. I'm slow, the other apprentices are nineteen and quicker than me. If the builder runs out of work before I'm qualified, that's three years wasted. That's my worry.

S0.say: I'm glad I learned a trade, because it was never going to be a computer putting a roof on. I'd say it to the lads on site and my old mates from the warehouse.
S0.think: It'd make me feel I made the right call, because I took a pay cut and everyone said I was mad at my age. If nothing changes, I've got time to finish, qualify and start earning properly.
S0.do: Carries on with the apprenticeship and completes his level two. Keeps living at home for two more years, saving about a hundred a month, and plans to go self-employed with his cousin once qualified.
S0.feel: Calm and even glad, feeling his choice is confirmed.
S0.quote: My grandad was a carpenter back home, and he always said a man with a trade never goes hungry.
S0.fieldNote: Felix made a deliberate, costly choice to learn a trade late, and a stall would confirm it. He is aware younger apprentices are quicker. His grandfather's saying is the backbone of how he sees work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Yeah, that's one I'd want to think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn a trade, because the office jobs will go before the hands-on ones. I'd say the government should put money into apprenticeships, not just universities. That's what I'd say to anyone, it's what I believe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry a bit about the trusses. They're made in a factory already, and if they start making whole roof sections, there's less for us on site. But someone still has to put them up, so I don't think it'd finish me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the apprenticeship and watch what the bigger firms start using. When the site gets the new kit, I'd want to learn it, but I'm not going to buy anything myself first. I'd use the AI apps a bit more for college, now the tutor's started using them too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A small worry, not a big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't buy anything first. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've got three weeks' money and a lot of things are hyped. My old warehouse bought a scanner system that was meant to change everything, and it was gone in a year. I'd rather see it working on someone else's site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about your going self-employed plan in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still want to, but maybe later. If the work's changing, I'd want to stay employed a bit longer and learn how the bigger firms do it. Then go out on my own when I know what I'm doing.

S1.say: Learn a trade, because office jobs will go before hands-on ones. The government should put money into apprenticeships, not just universities.
S1.think: I'd worry a bit about the trusses, because they're already factory-made and whole roof sections could follow. But someone still has to put them up, so I don't think it'd finish me.
S1.do: Keeps going with the apprenticeship and watches what bigger firms adopt, learning new kit when the site brings it in. Uses AI apps more for college now his tutor does, and delays his self-employment plan to learn from larger firms.
S1.feel: Uneasy, a small worry rather than a big one.
S1.quote: My old warehouse bought a scanner system that was meant to change everything, and it was gone in a year.
S1.fieldNote: Felix's steady streak shows in waiting to see equipment work elsewhere first, backed by a real story from his warehouse days. He champions apprenticeships over universities. He'd postpone going self-employed rather than abandon it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Hang on. I wouldn't even be qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's being forced on people too fast, and the companies doing it should slow down. I'm not one for big government, but someone has to make sure working people aren't left with nothing. I'd say it straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I've thrown away my warehouse job for nothing. Three years of apprentice pay, and a robot is putting the trusses up before I've got my certificate. And the warehouse would be robots by then too, so there's no going back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with my parents and work out how long I can keep paying board. I'd look at the jobs that need a person to be trusted, like the fire service, my dad's mate's a firefighter, and apply in the first year. I'd cut out everything extra, no saving up for a car, no nights out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gutted. Proper sick in the stomach, and I'd lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the fire service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I think people want a person running into a burning house, not a machine, at least at first. And it's a steady wage with a pension, and it's a bit like site work, you work as a team. I don't know if they'd take me, but I'd try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say sorry, probably. She was right about the money. Then she'd say don't be silly, you're home, we'll manage. Family's what you fall back on, that's how we were raised.

S2.say: It's being forced on people too fast, and the companies doing it should slow down. I'm not one for big government, but someone has to make sure working people aren't left with nothing.
S2.think: I'd think I threw away my warehouse job for nothing: three years of apprentice pay and a robot putting trusses up before I qualify. The warehouse would be robots too, so there's no going back.
S2.do: Sits down with his parents to work out how long he can keep paying board. Applies to the fire service in the first year and cuts all extras, including saving for a car and nights out.
S2.feel: Gutted, sick in the stomach and losing sleep.
S2.quote: Three years of apprentice pay, and a robot is putting the trusses up before I've got my certificate.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture hits Felix's big life decision directly, and his first impulse is to apologise to his mother. He looks for work where people want a trusted human, like the fire service. Family support is his natural fallback, as he was raised to expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Right. I'd be qualified by then, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to back apprenticeships and small businesses, so people can earn their way. I'd say the companies making money from robots should pay into training. That's fair, isn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I get maybe three good years as a qualified carpenter, then have to change. That's not nothing, but it's not what I gave up the warehouse for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship as fast as I can, maybe ask to do extra college days. I'd keep living at home and save harder, two hundred a month once I'm qualified. And once I saw a few people doing it, I'd take a course in setting up or maintaining site robots, because someone's going to have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it feels like I can still steer it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn robot maintenance once others did. Who would you want to see do it first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The site manager, or one of the older carpenters. If Steve, he's fifty and does nothing new, starts on it, then I know it's serious. Steve's like a weather forecast for change on our site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still go self-employed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. With five years, I'd rather stay with a bigger firm that's investing in the kit. Self-employed with no robots against firms with robots isn't a fair fight.

S3.say: This is the time to back apprenticeships and small businesses so people can earn their way. The companies making money from robots should pay into training, and that's fair.
S3.think: I'd get maybe three good years as a qualified carpenter, then have to change. That's not nothing, but it's not what I gave up the warehouse for.
S3.do: Finishes his apprenticeship as fast as possible, asking for extra college days, keeps living at home and saves 200 a month once qualified. Takes a course in setting up or maintaining site robots once he sees others doing it.
S3.feel: Anxious but still feeling able to steer.
S3.quote: Steve's like a weather forecast for change on our site.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Felix plans a path through qualification to robot maintenance, but only once a cautious older colleague moves first. He drops the self-employment dream as unrealistic against firms with robots. His view that companies should fund training sits alongside his dislike of big government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a proper career's worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do it right, so let people work and learn on the job. More apprenticeships in the new trades, not handouts. Same as I always say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I made the right call after all. I'd get seven or eight years as a carpenter, maybe run my own small firm, and still have time to learn the robot side. The end bothers me, but it's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship, move out of my parents' in three years, and maybe go self-employed with Jun after all. I'd save steadily and wait till robots are cheap and proven before buying one for the business. I'd learn whatever AI tools the trade's using as they come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, quietly. Mostly I'd feel all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In the two-year picture you'd apologise to your mum. What would you say to her here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say see, I told you. Nicely. She'd say don't get cocky. That's how it'd go in our kitchen, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change any personal plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to get married one day, but I'm single now, so that's not exactly a plan. I'd want my own place first. Ten years gives me time for that, at least.

S4.say: There's time to do it right, so let people work and learn on the job. More apprenticeships in the new trades, not handouts.
S4.think: I'd think I made the right call after all: seven or eight years as a carpenter, maybe my own small firm, and still time to learn the robot side. The end bothers me, but it's a long way off.
S4.do: Finishes the apprenticeship, moves out of his parents' home within three years and may go self-employed with his cousin. Saves steadily, waits until robots are cheap and proven before buying one for the business and learns AI tools as the trade adopts them.
S4.feel: Quietly uneasy but mostly all right.
S4.quote: I'd say see, I told you. Nicely. She'd say don't get cocky.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years revives Felix's self-employment plan and his sense of having chosen well. He'd still wait for robots to be proven before investing. The family kitchen exchange shows warmth and humour under the worry.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd have given up a steady job, done three years on apprentice pay and have nothing to show for it. What would help is the government and the big firms backing apprenticeships properly, paying people to learn the trades that are still needed, and support for families helping each other, not just benefits.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about people who started late. Everyone talks about school leavers, but there's lots of us who switched in our twenties. We've taken a pay cut to do the right thing, and we'd get hit the hardest.

headlineQuote: We've taken a pay cut to do the right thing, and we'd get hit the hardest.
portrait: Felix Chen is a 27-year-old first-year apprentice carpenter on a retirement village build who left eight years of warehouse work to learn a trade, living with his parents and paying board on about three weeks of savings. He's traditional, values apprenticeships and family over handouts, and waits for proof before trying new things, using AI now and then for college maths. A stall confirms his choice; steady change makes him watch others first. AGI by 2028 alarms him and he'd look to the fire service, while five and ten years let him finish his trade, then learn robot maintenance or start a small firm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have given up a steady job and done three years on apprentice pay with nothing to show for it.
whatWouldHelp: Government and big firms properly backing apprenticeships in trades still needed, and support for families helping each other rather than benefits.
